passage:
“Before you press share, tell me one thing,” Vidya Masi said. “Why are you posting it?”
Mahima looked at her sketch of the monsoon terrace. “I want people to see it.”
“Which people?”
“Not everyone.” She frowned. “Amma, Nani, my friends from class. Not strangers who say weird things about my drawings.”
“So who should be able to see it?”
“Only people I know. Which means a private account, not a public one.” She flipped the settings on her phone, laughing as she switched on approval for followers. “And I only post art. No location, no school uniform, no midnight selfies.”
“Sounds like a plan.”
“It's my plan. I made it.”

qa.q: Who does Mahima want to see her art?
qa.a: Mahima wants Amma, Nani and her friends from class to see it.

qa.q: What does Mahima's reply, It's my plan, I made it, suggest she feels?
qa.a: Mahima feels proud and independent, since she worked out the purpose and the rules herself.

qa.q: What could Mahima do if a stranger asks to follow?
qa.a: She could decline or ignore the request and keep the account private, since her purpose is to share with people she knows.

qa.q: How might Nani see Mahima's private account?
qa.a: Nani may feel happy and included, since she is one of the chosen viewers and can enjoy the art safely.

grounding: A teen asks why she is posting, chooses to share art with friends and family only and makes the account private so purpose shapes what goes up.

subtype: Approach: deciding purpose and audience first [Thinking]
passage:
When I made my art account last year, the first thing I did wasn't posting. I'm Sarita, and I sat on the stairs with my phone and asked myself: why am I doing this?
To get famous? No, that made my stomach knot. To sell drawings? Not yet. The honest answer was that I wanted Nani in Jaipur and my cousins to see what I make, and maybe a few friends from school to say something nice.
Once I knew that, the rest was easy. If the audience is family and friends, the account should be private. So I set it to private and only accepted people I actually know. My brother Santosh said I'd never get followers that way. I said, “I don't want followers. I want Nani.”
It also changed what I post: finished pieces and messy sketches, but no selfies, no school uniform, nothing about where we live.

qa.q: Who did Sarita want to see the art?
qa.a: Nani in Jaipur, the cousins, and a few friends from school.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel about the idea of getting famous?
qa.a: It made Sarita's stomach knot, a sign of discomfort with a big public audience.

qa.q: What else could Sarita decide as the account grows?
qa.a: Review every few months whether the purpose has changed, say toward selling, and adjust privacy only after talking it over with family.

qa.q: How does Santosh see the private account?
qa.a: Santosh thinks it limits followers, not seeing that Sarita's purpose is family, not fame.

grounding: Shows a teen asking why to post at all, choosing to share art with family and friends only, and setting the account to private so the purpose shapes what goes up.

passage:
Art teacher's note, Tuesday
Kashish asked me after class whether she should put her sketches online, because her friend Tanuja has a public account with thousands of followers. Instead of answering, I asked her why she wanted to post at all.
She thought for a while. Then she said the truth was that she wanted her grandparents in Shillong to see her progress, and a few classmates who like drawing. Not strangers. Not numbers.
Once she had said it aloud, she worked out the rest herself: if that's the audience, the account should be private, and she would accept only people she knows. She also decided not to post her face or anything showing the school, since that doesn't serve the purpose.
She set it up on her phone before leaving the art room. I suggested she show her parents the settings tonight. Next week I will ask how her grandparents liked the first sketch.

qa.q: What did Kashish want most from posting, once she thought about it?
qa.a: Kashish wanted her grandparents and a few classmates to see her progress, and felt uninterested in strangers or numbers.

qa.q: What else could Kashish do to keep the account true to its purpose?
qa.a: Check followers now and then, removing anyone she doesn't know, and keep showing her parents the settings.

qa.q: How might Tanuja's public account differ from Kashish's plan?
qa.a: Tanuja's account seeks many followers, while Kashish's aims at a small, known audience, so they suit different purposes.

grounding: A teacher notes a teen asking why she wants to post, choosing family and a few classmates as her audience, and setting her art account to private.
